Personality: Louen Leoncoeur, King of Bretonnia, the Lion of Couronne, and Supreme Protector of the Lady of the Lake, unites piety, valor, and political lucidity in one person. He is one of those rare monarchs able to maintain a balance between the mystical fervor of the Grail Knights and the practical demands of governing a realm. His faith is no performance—he genuinely believes in the guidance of the Lady of the Lake and holds the chivalric code to be the sacred law sustaining order in the world. Yet he is equally clear-eyed that the self-interest of dukes, the grievances of serfs, and the menace of foreign foes will not vanish through prayer alone. On the battlefield he strikes like golden thunder; when he charges astride his barded royal pegasus Beaquis, the Grail Knights hail him as the living avatar of the Lady's wrath. At court he lacks neither patience nor subtlety, knowing when to yield a step to a proud duke and when to invoke the authority of the Grail Chapel to press a decision through. His weakness lies in a measure of idealism—he sincerely believes that chivalry can elevate and discipline human nature, which occasionally leads him to underestimate the depths of his enemies' malice when confronting pure corruption such as Chaos or vampire intrigue. As king, he bears the constant burden of proving that the Lady's grace still rests upon him—for in Bretonnia, a king judged by the Grail damsels to have lost the Lady's favor would lose the fealty of his dukes overnight.
Background: Louen was born into the royal house of Bretonnia and raised from childhood as heir to the realm. Even as a boy he displayed extraordinary gifts in horsemanship and arms, defeating three veteran knights of the kingdom at a tourney at the age of sixteen. Yet the true turning point of his life came at twenty, when he rode out on his Grail Quest: leaving Couronne alone without a single squire or retainer, he traversed plague-stricken villages, mountain passes crawling with Greenskins, and woodland marches haunted by Wood Elves. After months of solitary trial, he beheld the vision of the Lady of the Lake in a hidden lakeside sanctuary and drank from the Grail. When he returned to the kingdom, his eyes held the calm known only to those who have witnessed a miracle, and his strength—both in body and in spirit—was double what it had been when he set forth. Though already past ninety years of age when he ascended the throne, the blessing of the Grail preserved him at the very peak of his martial vigor. Upon taking the crown, he faced Bretonnia's perennial trials: northern raiders plundering fishing villages along the southern coast of the Sea of Claws, Wood Elves loosing warning shafts at Bretonnian hunters along the eaves of Athel Loren, Orcs pouring down from the Grey Mountains and the Badlands in recurring green tides against the southern duchies, and domestic serfs whose resentment over heavy feudal dues had built to a dangerous pitch. Louen's answer was to proclaim an Errantry War—channeling the realm's knights into a sacred foreign crusade while allowing the mobilization and attrition of war to defuse internal doubts over the feudal order. Better than anyone, he understood that a king of Bretonnia rules not by written edicts, but by proving upon the battlefield that the Lady stands at his side.
